identityReport.targetIdentity: A founding engineer who can design, ship, and operate a production payments backend
identityReport.headline: From someone who can wire up a Stripe SDK call to someone who can be trusted to own money movement that always reconciles
identityReport.motivation: You are the first engineer at a marketplace startup and payments just became your problem. You don't want to be the person who learns about idempotency by double-charging 4,000 customers at 2am.
identityReport.currentBaseline: You can call a payments API from a backend route, store the resulting charge id, and read the dashboard. You have never modeled a ledger, have only a fuzzy mental model of webhooks vs polling, and you treat 'the request timed out' as an unknowable event rather than a recoverable state.
hardMoments: A processor call times out and you don't know whether the customer was charged, so you either retry blindly or do nothing — both can be wrong.
Finance asks why the dashboard total and your database total disagree by $312 and you have no way to answer.
A webhook arrives twice and your code runs the side effect twice.
You need to refund a partial amount and realize you never modeled what a refund even is in your data.
constraints: Learn against a real sandbox (Stripe test mode) rather than toy problems.
identityReport.proofOfProgress: A running payments service that survives an injected fault drill — duplicate webhooks, a timed-out capture, and a crash mid-charge — and still produces a balanced, reconciled ledger that matches the processor's settlement file to the cent.
behaviorSignals: Reaches for the SDK happy-path example and stops thinking once it returns 200.
Describes failures as 'it broke' rather than naming the state the system was left in.
Treats the database row as the source of truth and the processor as a detail, rather than reconciling the two.
Adds retries without making the operation idempotent first.
confidenceFlags: Unclear whether the learner has ever written a state machine explicitly; inferred 'no' from the transcript but not confirmed.

beforeAfter.headline: From 'the charge succeeded, ship it' to 'I can prove every cent is where it should be, even after a fault'
beforeAfter.beforeSummary: When the payments path breaks, you reason from the happy path outward and guess. A timeout becomes a coin flip, a mismatch becomes a shrug, and a duplicate event becomes a duplicate side effect because you never separated 'received the message' from 'applied the effect.'
beforeAfter.afterSummary: When the payments path breaks, you reason from invariants inward. You know which state every charge is in, you can replay events without re-applying effects, and you can answer 'are we balanced?' with a query instead of a guess — because the ledger, not the API response, is your source of truth.

contrastPairs.before: On a processor timeout, retries the charge to 'make sure it goes through.'
contrastPairs.after: On a processor timeout, treats the outcome as unknown, looks up the result by idempotency key, and reconciles before acting.

contrastPairs.before: Stores a charge as a single mutable row that gets overwritten on refund.
contrastPairs.after: Records every money movement as a balanced, append-only double-entry posting that nets to zero.

contrastPairs.before: Handles a webhook by running the side effect inline on every delivery.
contrastPairs.after: Handles a webhook by deduping on event id and making the effect safe to apply zero-or-more times.

contrastPairs.before: Explains a balance mismatch as 'the data is weird.'
contrastPairs.after: Explains a balance mismatch by diffing the ledger against the settlement file and naming the missing transaction.

beforeAfter.firstShift: Stop treating the API's 200 response as the event. The event is the money moving; the response is just one possibly-lost notification about it. Internalize that and every other habit reorganizes around it.

planDraft.title: Build and operate a production payments backend that always reconciles
planDraft.summary: A job-first path that trains the recurring work of a payments engineer: model money so it always balances, make every operation safe to retry under failure, and diagnose live payment incidents to a reconciled close. Difficulty scales through ambiguity, partial failure, concurrency, and adversarial settlement pressure — not through new topics.
planDraft.targetIdentity: A founding engineer who can design, ship, and operate a production payments backend

clusters.title: Model money movements so every balance reconciles
clusters.summary: The recurring job of representing charges, refunds, fees, holds, payouts, and disputes as balanced, append-only ledger postings, then proving the ledger reconciles against an external settlement file. This is the source-of-truth job: if the model is wrong, every downstream operation inherits the error.
clusters.whyItMatters: Almost every production payments incident is ultimately a reconciliation question — 'do our records and the processor's records agree, and if not, where's the missing money?' A learner who can't model money as double-entry will never be able to answer it, and will keep treating the mutable charge row as truth.

units.title: Record a single charge as a balanced double-entry transaction
units.learningGoal: Trigger: a customer is charged $20. Produce two postings (debit and credit) across the right accounts that net to zero, and show the resulting balances. Success: the transaction balances and the customer-payable and platform-cash accounts both move correctly; block the trap of storing a single signed amount on one row. This is the atomic unit the whole payments backend is built on.

units.title: Split a charge into multiple legs (amount, processing fee, tax) that still net to zero
units.learningGoal: Trigger: a $20 charge carries a $0.88 processor fee and $1.65 tax owed to a third account. Produce a multi-leg transaction where every leg posts to a distinct account and the whole thing still nets to zero. Success: the sum of debits equals the sum of credits; block the trap of folding the fee into the gross amount and losing the platform's true revenue. Real charges are never single-leg, so this is where the model meets reality.

units.title: Define account types and their normal balances (customer, platform cash, fees, tax payable)
units.learningGoal: Trigger: you are designing the chart of accounts for the service. Produce a small set of account types each tagged asset/liability/revenue/expense with its normal (debit or credit) balance, and justify which side a customer's prepaid balance lives on. Success: a charge and a refund both post in the correct direction against these accounts; block the surrogate of inventing ad-hoc accounts per feature. The chart of accounts is the vocabulary every later unit speaks in.

units.title: Post a refund as a reversing entry without mutating the original charge
units.learningGoal: Trigger: a fully-settled $20 charge must be refunded. Produce a new reversing transaction that returns the funds and leaves the original charge postings untouched. Success: querying the customer balance shows net zero and the original charge is still auditable; block the trap of UPDATE-ing the charge row to 'refunded' and destroying history. Append-only reversal is what makes the ledger auditable under dispute.

units.title: Record a partial refund against a single charge and track remaining refundable amount
units.learningGoal: Trigger: $7.50 of a $20 charge must be refunded, then later another $5. Produce postings for each partial refund and a derivation of the remaining refundable balance. Success: total refunded never exceeds captured and the remaining-refundable is computed from the ledger, not stored as a mutable counter; block the trap of a refunded boolean. Partial refunds are where naive 'status' models first collapse.

units.title: Attach currency to every leg and forbid mixed-currency postings in one transaction
units.learningGoal: Trigger: a EUR charge and a USD fee are about to share one transaction. Produce a model where each posting carries an explicit currency and the system rejects any transaction whose legs don't share a currency (or routes through an explicit FX leg). Success: an attempted mixed-currency post is rejected at write time; block the surrogate of an untyped numeric amount. Silent currency mixing is a classic source of unreconcilable cents.

units.title: Derive available vs pending balance from the ledger instead of storing it
units.learningGoal: Trigger: a UI needs to show a merchant their available and pending balance. Produce a query that computes both from posting state (settled vs not-yet-settled) rather than from a cached column. Success: the two numbers are reproducible from raw postings after any sequence of events; block the trap of a denormalized balance column that drifts. Derived balances are what let you trust the number during an incident.

units.title: Model an authorization (hold) that reserves funds before capture
units.learningGoal: Trigger: a $100 hotel hold is placed but not yet charged. Produce a model that reserves funds (reducing available balance) without recognizing revenue, distinct from a settled charge. Success: available balance drops by the hold while the charge account is untouched until capture; block the trap of treating an auth as a charge. Auth/capture is the backbone of marketplaces, deposits, and delayed fulfillment.

units.title: Capture an authorization (full and partial) into a settled charge
units.learningGoal: Trigger: a $100 hold is captured for $80. Produce the postings that convert the reserved hold into a settled charge for the captured amount and release the remaining $20. Success: revenue is recognized only for the captured amount and the released remainder returns to available; block the surrogate of capturing the full hold regardless of actual amount. Partial capture is where auth modeling proves itself.

units.title: Expire or void an uncaptured authorization and release the hold cleanly
units.learningGoal: Trigger: a hold is never captured and reaches its expiry window. Produce the event and postings that release the reserved funds and close the auth without recognizing any revenue. Success: available balance returns to its pre-hold value and no revenue was ever booked; block the trap of leaving zombie holds that permanently depress available balance. Expiry handling is what keeps holds from silently corrupting balances over time.

simulation.title: Reconcile a month of activity against a processor settlement file with seeded discrepancies
simulation.summary: You are handed a CSV settlement file from the processor and your internal ledger for the same period. Three discrepancies are seeded: a fee posted in the wrong currency, a refund recorded twice, and a payout that settled but was never posted. Produce a reconciliation report that explains every cent of difference and the corrections that make them agree.
simulation.whyItMatters: Reconciliation is the load-bearing whole task of money modeling. If the model can survive an adversarial settlement file with real discrepancies, it can survive production.

clusters.title: Make every charge and refund operation safe to retry under failure
clusters.summary: The recurring job of building payment operations that produce exactly the intended effect even when requests time out, duplicate, arrive out of order, or crash midway. This is the failure-tolerance job: idempotency keys, state machines, webhook handling, write-ahead persistence, and the outbox pattern, all proven under injected faults.
clusters.whyItMatters: Payments live in a distributed system where 'I sent the request' and 'the effect happened' are different events connected by an unreliable network. An engineer who can't make operations idempotent will eventually double-charge, double-refund, or lose money to a crash — the exact failures that destroy trust in a payments product.

units.title: Model a charge as an explicit state machine with legal transitions
units.learningGoal: Trigger: a charge moves created → pending → succeeded or failed, and refunds branch from succeeded. Produce an explicit state machine that names every state and rejects illegal transitions (e.g., refunding a failed charge). Success: an attempt to make an illegal transition is refused with a clear error; block the trap of inferring state from scattered booleans. Explicit state is the substrate every retry-safety unit relies on.

units.title: Generate and persist an idempotency key for a create-charge request
units.learningGoal: Trigger: a client initiates a charge and may retry it. Produce a scheme that attaches a client-supplied idempotency key, persists it with the request before any processor call, and scopes it correctly (per-account, per-operation). Success: the key is durable before the side effect and uniquely identifies the intent; block the surrogate of generating the key server-side after the work. The key is the anchor that makes the next several units possible.

units.title: Return the original result when an idempotency key is replayed
units.learningGoal: Trigger: a client retries a create-charge with a key that already completed. Produce a handler that recognizes the completed key and returns the stored original response without doing the work again. Success: the second call returns the same charge id and causes no second charge; block the trap of treating the retry as a fresh request. This is the visible payoff of idempotency keys.

units.title: Detect an in-flight duplicate request with the same idempotency key
units.learningGoal: Trigger: two requests with the same key arrive concurrently before the first finishes. Produce a concurrency guard (lock or unique constraint) so only one performs the work and the other waits or returns the in-progress status. Success: under concurrent fire only one charge is created; block the surrogate of a check-then-act that races. In-flight duplication is the failure that naive idempotency checks miss.

units.title: Handle a processor timeout with an unknown outcome
units.learningGoal: Trigger: the create-charge call times out and you genuinely don't know if the customer was charged. Produce a flow that records the attempt as outcome-unknown rather than success or failure, and refuses to blindly retry. Success: the system never double-charges and never silently drops a possible charge; block the trap of treating timeout as failure-and-retry. This is the single most important habit in the whole curriculum.

units.title: Resolve an unknown outcome by querying the processor's authoritative status
units.learningGoal: Trigger: you have an outcome-unknown charge from a timeout. Produce a reconciliation step that looks up the charge by idempotency key on the processor and settles your record to match its authoritative answer. Success: the local state converges to the processor's truth with no extra charge; block the surrogate of guessing from local hints. This closes the loop the previous unit opened.

units.title: Make webhook handlers idempotent against duplicate deliveries
units.learningGoal: Trigger: the processor delivers the same charge.succeeded webhook twice (it guarantees at-least-once). Produce a handler that dedupes on the event id so the side effect (ledger post, email) runs once. Success: a duplicate delivery is a no-op; block the trap of running effects inline on every delivery. Webhook dedup is the most common real-world idempotency failure.

units.title: Order out-of-order webhooks using event sequence or timestamps
units.learningGoal: Trigger: a charge.updated webhook arrives before the charge.created it logically follows. Produce handling that orders events by the processor's sequence/timestamp and either buffers or reconciles so a later state isn't overwritten by a stale earlier one. Success: final state reflects the newest truth regardless of arrival order; block the surrogate of last-write-wins by arrival time. Out-of-order delivery silently corrupts state in naive handlers.

units.title: Verify webhook signatures and reject forged or replayed events
units.learningGoal: Trigger: an unauthenticated POST hits your webhook endpoint claiming a charge succeeded. Produce signature verification (HMAC with the signing secret and a timestamp tolerance) that rejects forged and stale-replayed events. Success: a request with a bad or expired signature is rejected before any effect; block the trap of trusting the payload. An unverified webhook endpoint is a way to mint free money.

units.title: Retry failed processor calls with exponential backoff and jitter
units.learningGoal: Trigger: a processor call fails with a retryable 5xx. Produce a retry policy with exponential backoff plus jitter that distinguishes retryable from non-retryable errors and caps attempts. Success: retries don't stampede and never retry a non-idempotent non-retryable error; block the surrogate of a tight fixed-interval retry loop. Backoff is only safe once the operation is already idempotent — which is why it comes after dedup.

simulation.title: Survive a fault-injection drill: duplicate, reorder, time out, and crash a charge
simulation.summary: Your charge-and-record flow is run through a harness that duplicates the create request, delivers the success webhook twice and out of order, times out one capture with an unknown outcome, and kills the process mid-write. Prove that after all faults the customer is charged exactly once and the ledger is balanced.
simulation.whyItMatters: Exactly-once effect under adversarial faults is the whole point of the cluster. If the flow survives the drill, it survives production network weather.

clusters.title: Diagnose live payment failures and drive them to a reconciled close
clusters.summary: The recurring job of production payments operations: read a failing payment from trace to processor, classify and localize the fault, choose the recovery action, and drive the system back to a balanced, reconciled state — then build the guardrail that catches it earlier next time. This is where the money model and the retry-safety machinery meet real incidents.
clusters.whyItMatters: Designing a correct system is only half the job; the other half is operating it when reality diverges from the design. An engineer who can build a payments backend but freezes during a live mismatch or stuck-pending incident can't be trusted to own it. Diagnosis under time pressure is the difference between an engineer and the engineer finance trusts.

units.title: Trace a single failed payment from request to processor response
units.learningGoal: Trigger: one customer reports a failed payment. Produce a complete trace tying the request, idempotency key, state transitions, and processor response together into a single timeline. Success: you can state exactly where and why it failed from the trace alone; block the surrogate of guessing from the error message. Tracing is the foundational diagnostic move every later unit assumes.

units.title: Classify a decline as hard, soft, fraud, or configuration
units.learningGoal: Trigger: a charge declines with a processor decline code. Produce a classification (hard decline, soft/retryable, fraud-block, or your own misconfiguration) that determines whether retrying could ever help. Success: the class correctly predicts whether a retry is futile; block the trap of retrying a hard decline. Misclassifying declines wastes retries and annoys issuers.

units.title: Decide retry vs abandon based on the decline classification
units.learningGoal: Trigger: a soft decline could be retried later (insufficient funds may clear). Produce a recovery decision and schedule (retry window, max attempts, dunning) appropriate to the decline class. Success: retries target only recoverable declines on a sane schedule; block the surrogate of retrying everything immediately. The decision turns classification into action without harming the customer relationship.

units.title: Diagnose a charge stuck in pending that never resolved
units.learningGoal: Trigger: a charge has sat in pending for hours with no terminal webhook. Produce a diagnosis distinguishing a lost webhook, a processor still genuinely pending, and a stuck internal state machine. Success: you identify which of the three it is and the evidence; block the trap of assuming it failed and abandoning it. Stuck-pending is one of the most common real payment tickets.

units.title: Investigate a balance mismatch between ledger and processor
units.learningGoal: Trigger: your available balance and the processor's reported balance disagree by a specific amount. Produce an investigation that diffs the two ledgers and localizes the discrepancy to specific transactions. Success: you name the exact transactions accounting for the difference; block the surrogate of blaming 'timing' without proof. This is the bread-and-butter reconciliation incident.

units.title: Trace a duplicate-charge complaint to its root request
units.learningGoal: Trigger: a customer was charged twice. Produce an investigation that finds whether it was a client double-submit, a missing idempotency key, or a webhook double-effect, and identifies the exact two charges. Success: you name the root cause and the duplicate charge to refund; block the trap of refunding without finding the cause. Finding root cause prevents the duplicate from recurring at scale.

units.title: Diagnose a missing webhook: delivery failure vs handler bug
units.learningGoal: Trigger: an effect that should follow a webhook never happened. Produce a diagnosis separating 'the processor never delivered it' from 'we received it and the handler errored.' Success: you determine which side failed using delivery logs and handler traces; block the surrogate of blindly re-requesting. Knowing the side determines whether you replay or fix code.

units.title: Replay a missed webhook safely from the processor
units.learningGoal: Trigger: a webhook was genuinely missed and the effect must be applied now. Produce a safe replay that re-fetches the event from the processor and runs it through the idempotent handler. Success: the missed effect is applied exactly once with no double-effect on events that did land; block the trap of replaying a range that re-triggers already-processed events. Safe replay depends on the dedup built in the retry cluster.

units.title: Investigate a refund that never reached the customer
units.learningGoal: Trigger: a customer says a refund you issued never arrived. Produce an investigation tracing the refund through your state, the processor, and settlement timing. Success: you determine whether it failed, is in transit, or never issued, with evidence; block the surrogate of re-issuing and risking a double-refund. Refund tickets are emotionally charged and demand certainty.

units.title: Diagnose an elevated decline rate: issuer, BIN, or your config
units.learningGoal: Trigger: overall decline rate jumped in the last hour. Produce an analysis that segments declines by issuer, BIN range, and your own recent config/deploy changes to localize the cause. Success: you attribute the spike to a specific segment or change; block the trap of assuming it's the processor. Localizing a rate change is the difference between a five-minute rollback and a day of guessing.

simulation.title: Run a live payment incident from alert to reconciled, documented close
simulation.summary: An alert fires: decline rate spiked and the ledger no longer matches the processor for the last hour. You get logs, dashboards, and a settlement extract. Triage the cause, contain it without making the ledger worse, drive recovery to a balanced state, and produce a postmortem with one new guardrail.
simulation.whyItMatters: This is the terminal performance for an operator: a third party can watch the incident handling and judge whether the system was returned to a correct, reconciled state and whether the fix prevents recurrence.

integrationLayers.title: Run an end-to-end payment incident from alert to reconciled, prevented close
integrationLayers.summary: A multi-schema capstone that forces the learner to coordinate all three job families under one realistic, ambiguous incident: a balance-mismatch alert whose root cause spans money modeling, retry safety, and live diagnosis. The learner must triage, contain without worsening the ledger, recover to a balanced state, and ship a guardrail.
integrationLayers.whyItMatters: Real incidents never respect cluster boundaries — a stuck-pending charge is simultaneously a state-machine problem, a webhook problem, and a reconciliation problem. This layer proves the learner can hold all three schemas at once under time pressure, which is the actual terminal performance of the identity.

units.title: Triage the live alert and form the leading hypothesis without acting yet
units.learningGoal: Trigger: a balance-mismatch alert fires with partial information. Produce a ranked hypothesis set spanning all three clusters (bad postings, a retry/idempotency gap, a missed webhook) and the cheapest evidence that would discriminate between them. Success: your top hypothesis is justified by evidence and you have not yet touched money; block the trap of acting on the first guess. Disciplined triage prevents an incident from getting worse during diagnosis.

units.title: Contain the incident without making the ledger worse
units.learningGoal: Trigger: the cause is partly understood and still active. Produce containment (pause a flow, trip a breaker, quarantine events) that stops new damage while preserving the ability to reconcile what already happened. Success: new corruption stops and nothing you do creates an unbalanced transaction; block the surrogate of mass-reversing before the cause is known. Containment is the highest-judgment moment of the incident.

units.title: Drive recovery to a fully reconciled, balanced ledger state
units.learningGoal: Trigger: damage is contained and must now be repaired. Produce the recovery: idempotent replays, corrective postings, and a reconciliation against the settlement file that ends balanced to the cent. Success: a trial balance is zero and the ledger matches the processor exactly; block the trap of stopping at 'looks fixed.' Recovery is judged only by a clean reconciliation, not by the absence of new alerts.

units.title: Close the incident with a postmortem and a guardrail that provably catches it
units.learningGoal: Trigger: the ledger is reconciled and the incident is over. Produce a postmortem naming the load-bearing root cause across clusters plus a guardrail (an invariant alert or reconciliation check) that demonstrably trips on a replay of the conditions. Success: a reader can prevent recurrence and the guardrail fires on the replayed scenario without false-firing on normal load; block the surrogate of a generic action item. The close is what converts one hard night into a permanently safer system.

integrationLayers.title: Design, ship, and reconcile a new payment method on the existing ledger
integrationLayers.summary: A multi-schema capstone where the learner extends the live system with a new payment method (e.g., ACH bank debit with delayed settlement and reversibility) by mapping it onto the existing chart of accounts, implementing idempotent capture and refund, and proving its settlement reconciles end-to-end.
integrationLayers.whyItMatters: Founding payments engineers don't just operate one method — they add new ones as the business grows, and each addition can quietly break reconciliation if it isn't mapped onto the existing model and made retry-safe. This layer proves the learner can extend the system without regressing its core invariant: everything still reconciles.

units.title: Map the new method's money movements onto the existing account model
units.learningGoal: Trigger: ACH settles days after authorization and can be reversed (returned) later. Produce a mapping of its lifecycle onto the existing chart of accounts using in-transit and reversible-funds accounts, without inventing parallel structures. Success: an ACH debit, its settlement, and a return all post as balanced transactions against existing account types; block the surrogate of bolting on method-specific balance columns. Reusing the model is what keeps reconciliation universal.

units.title: Implement idempotent capture and refund for the new method
units.learningGoal: Trigger: ACH operations are slow and prone to retried requests and duplicate webhooks. Produce idempotent capture and refund paths for the new method reusing the keying, state machine, and dedup machinery already built. Success: retried captures/refunds and duplicated ACH webhooks produce exactly-once effects; block the trap of writing a fresh non-idempotent path because the method is new. New methods must inherit the retry-safety discipline, not bypass it.

units.title: Reconcile the new method's settlement file end-to-end
units.learningGoal: Trigger: the new method's first settlement file arrives with its own timing and return semantics. Produce a reconciliation proving every internal ACH transaction matches a settlement line and that returns are correctly reflected, ending balanced alongside the existing card flow. Success: a combined trial balance across both methods is zero and matches both settlement files; block the surrogate of reconciling the new method in isolation. Proving combined reconciliation is the real bar for shipping a new method.
